description:
We are Team Pioneers9 and we are a passionate group of space enthusiasts and problem solvers driven by curiosity and innovation.

Our team brings together skills in software development and creative problem solving.  We absolutely love taking complex data sets and turn them into useful apps/widgets that the public would find easy to use.
summary: My team, Pioneers 9, has created a fundamental website: SPHEREx Sky Explorer. This is a free public-facing web tool that turns NASA SPHEREx images of any patch of the sky into a blink video, so anyone can see what moves or changes over time. Users of the website can enter a RA/Dec coordinate or pick one of the preset challenge targets, and this tool find every SPHEREx exposure, aligns them, and lets them blink, stack, subtract, and compare all six infrared detectors (0.75-5μm). Clicking any star gives its spectrum and light curve on the fly; a moving-object finder flags anything that moved an isn't a known Gaia or WISE stater. On real data it automatically found WISE 0855 moving 8.5''/yr (catalogue: 8.1''/yr), and its brightness measurements match 2MASS and WISE. It stayed working through outages of NASA's IRSA search by reading images straight from NASA's AWS copy. This matter because SPHEREs maps the whole sky every six months: nearby cold brown dwarfs and other unknown neighbours can now be found by anyone, not just specialists.
details:
SPHEREx Sky Explorer – https://spherexplorer-sky.study

Team Pioneers9: Rachit Banker (team owner) and Heng Jie Weng

What is it?

SPHEREx Sky Explorer is a free website that lets anyone look at the real images NASA's SPHEREx telescope has taken of any part of the sky, and find out what is moving or changing there. You type a position or a name, or click one of the challenge targets. The Explorer then finds every SPHEREx image of that spot, cuts out and lines up a small window from each one, and plays them as a blink video. Anything that jumps between frames is moving. Anything that brightens or fades is changing.

From the same images it then does what normally takes an astronomer a day of Python:

  • Measures the spectrum of any star in SPHEREx's 102 infrared colours (0.75–5 µm) and checks it for the signatures of a cold brown dwarf: methane at 3.3 µm, CO at 4.6 µm, no light below 2 µm.
  • Draws a light curve and searches it for a period, while stating honestly which other periods SPHEREx's widely spaced visits cannot rule out.
  • Runs a moving-object finder that compares the first and last visits, checks every mover against Gaia and WISE, and flags anything unexplained as a candidate. The finder writes a ready-to-send report.
  • Cross-checks each spectrum against SPHEREx's independent All-Sky Cube.

Everything is real SPHEREx data. It is compatible on a computer, tablet or phone.

How does it work?

  • Image search: IRSA's SIA service, covering DR1 and QR3 together. New releases are found automatically from NASA's AWS archive. If SIA fails it falls back to TAP async and then TAP sync, with retries.
  • Images: IRSA cutouts, or byte-range reads straight from NASA's public AWS (S3) copy of the archive. This uses our own RICE_1 decompressor and was checked pixel for pixel against IRSA's cutouts.
  • Alignment and timing: every frame is aligned on a shared grid using its own SIP astrometry and its per-pixel wavelength table. Each star is moved to each frame's date using its catalogue proper motion.
  • Measurements: PSF fits with neighbouring stars fitted at the same time. Error bars come from the same fit at around 200 empty spots in the image. SPHEREx's own quality flags remove hot pixels, ghosts and cosmic rays.
  • Resilience: when IRSA is overloaded, the five challenge targets keep working from saved image lists, with images taken from AWS. A status badge shows which data services are up.

Proof that it works (real SPHEREx data, checked 15 Nov 2026)

  • WISE 0855, the coldest known brown dwarf: invisible in detectors D1–D4 and detected in D5 and D6. D6 gives 412 ± 81 µJy, against roughly 480 µJy expected from WISE. The spectrum check says "methane absorption, very cold: late T or Y dwarf".
  • The moving-object finder found WISE 0855 on its own, moving 8.5″/yr west. The catalogue value is 8.1″/yr.
  • Barnard's Star at 2.25 µm: 10.7 Jy, against 10.5 Jy from 2MASS. Its saturation is detected automatically from SPHEREx's flags and the user is warned.
  • Epsilon Indi B: detected in all six detectors. The spectrum from individual frames and the All-Sky Cube agree, including the methane dip.
  • RW Aurigae and R Draconis: brightness changes of tens of percent between visits, as expected for a young star and a Mira variable.

Benefits and intended impact

  • SPHEREx maps the whole sky every six months. Most of its moving and changing objects will never be looked at by a professional. This tool lets students, amateurs and citizen scientists as well as professionals in the field of astrophysics and cosmology to search the data themselves.
  • Candidate reports are written so they can go straight to Backyard Worlds or an astronomer.
  • It needs no setup. A shared link reopens the exact view, and an embed code puts it in a classroom page or a museum display.
  • It is honest about limits. It warns when a star saturates, never calls a blended source more than "tentative", and lists period aliases instead of guessing.
  • It explains itself: a 2-minute guided tour, "What am I looking at?" for every view, and a 24-page illustrated starter guide.
  • It gets better on its own: each new SPHEREx release (DR2, QR4 and so on) is picked up automatically, so moving objects and periods become measurable as the visits add up.

How is it creative?

  • The website incorporates a 1930s idea in a 2026 digital 'telescope'. Clyde Tombaugh found Pluto by blinking photographic plates. We apply the same "blink" idea to a 102-colour infrared survey, so every blink also scans through wavelength.
  • Because each SPHEREx frame sees a slightly different colour, a light curve would normally mix up colour with variability. We divide each frame by the star's own spectrum at that wavelength, so only real changes remain.
  • We read NASA's archive straight from AWS, slicing just the bytes needed from compressed FITS files. That kept the tool working through IRSA outages during the hackathon itself.
  • A colour picture (D1 blue, D3 green, D6 red) makes cold brown dwarfs pop out as red dots.

Tools, languages, software the team used

  • Languages: Python and JavaScript (ES modules, no framework), HTML and CSS.
  • Backend: Flask, NumPy, astropy and gunicorn, in a Docker container on Google Cloud Run, on our own domain.
  • Viewer: Aladin Lite (CDS).
  • Data sources: NASA/IPAC IRSA (SIA, TAP, cutouts), the NASA SPHEREx AWS Open Data archive, Gaia DR3, CatWISE2020 and AllWISE (through IRSA and NOIRLab Astro Data Lab, with VizieR as backup), and SIMBAD/Sesame.
  • Things we wrote ourselves: the GIF encoder, the RICE_1 decompressor, HEALPix cube reading, Lomb–Scargle, and SAMP messaging to TOPCAT and Aladin Desktop, as well as crosschecking most of the code.
  • Testing: over 100 automated tests in Python and JavaScript, run on GitHub Actions, plus end-to-end browser tests with Playwright.
  • No special hardware is needed.
  • We used Claude (Anthropic), an AI assistant, to help analyse written code and documentation. We tested every scientific result against real data and published values.

What factors did the team consider?

  • Honesty over flashiness: real data only, error bars on everything, explicit warnings, no overclaimed detections.
  • Reliability: IRSA was overloaded during the challenge, so we added saved lists, AWS images, fast failure and a live status display.
  • Accessibility for beginners: plain-English labels, a tour, explanations and a guide.
  • Interoperability for experts: CSV and VOTable export, SAMP links to TOPCAT and Aladin, and links to IRSA's own tools.
  • Future-proofing: one settings file, automatic detection of new releases, and weekly automatic tests.

Version history

  • v0.1 – Sky viewer: Aladin Lite map, RA/Dec and name lookup, field of view, background surveys, the five challenge targets.
  • v0.2 – Find SPHEREx images at the map centre with IRSA SIA. v0.2.1: TAP as a backup search.
  • v0.3 – Blink player: cutouts aligned on a shared grid, cached and played as a video. v0.3.1: retries for a slow IRSA, saved lists, demo mode.
  • v0.4 – Proper-motion handling: sourced motions for all five targets and SIMBAD lookup for others. "Fixed sky" and "Follow target" modes, with a dashed ring at the predicted position. v0.4.1: refinements.
  • v0.5 – Stack, Difference and six-detector views. Artifacts are cleaned using SPHEREx flags, and each frame's real wavelength is used.
  • v0.6 – Gaia DR3 and CatWISE/AllWISE stars drawn on every frame, moved to each frame's date. Click a star for its details.
  • v0.6.6 – "Measure at target" with honest significance from empty spots. D5 + D6 combined stack. Smoothing for faint sources. "All frames" option. Progress bar with Cancel.
  • v0.6.7 – Blend warnings and a two-source PSF fit for targets next to other stars. Colour check and motion check.
  • v0.6.8 – Saved frames, image lists and star lists, so repeat views are instant and judges' views work even when IRSA is down. Pre-fill page.
  • v0.6.9–v0.6.10 (merged into v0.7.1) – Sturdier search: SIA, then TAP async, then TAP sync, with retries and Retry-After support.
  • v0.7 – Spectrum and light curve for any star you click: PSF photometry in every frame, wavelength read per pixel, CSV download, variability test. v0.7.1: the sturdier search above.
  • v0.8 – SPHEREx flags overlay (click a pixel to read its flags) and a Frame details panel. v0.8.1: images read straight from NASA's AWS archive, matching IRSA pixel for pixel.
  • v0.9 / v1.0 – Shareable links that reopen the exact view, embed code, links to IRSA's SPHEREx tools, NOIRLab Data Lab as a catalogue backup, a full polish pass.
  • v1.0.1 – Fast, clear failure when IRSA is down, instead of minute-long waits.
  • v1.0.2 – Importer for IRSA Spectrophotometry Tool tables. Saved image list for Barnard's Star. Saturation warning.
  • v1.0.3 – WISE 0855 image list. Permanently bad pixels (flag bit 6) now masked.
  • v1.0.4 – Epsilon Indi B image list. Detected in all six detectors.
  • v1.0.5 – RW Aurigae image list. Importer reads summary tables and VOTables. Warm-dust interpretation added.
  • v1.0.6 – R Draconis image list. All five targets now work from real data without IRSA's search.
  • v1.0.7 – Following IRSA help-desk advice: DR1 and QR3 searched together, with smarter retries. v1.0.7.1: loading percentage. v1.0.7.2: IRSA asked first for every search, and new data releases detected automatically. v1.0.7.3: full code review and fixes.
  • v1.1 – Settings file, live data-source status badge, VOTable export, "Send to TOPCAT/Aladin" (SAMP), All-Sky Cube comparison, Docker image and automatic tests. v1.1.1: fixes after testing.
  • v1.2 – Moving-object finder with candidate reports, automatic spectrum check (methane, CO, cold, dust), period finder with alias warnings, colour picture, GIF download, guided tour and "What am I looking at?".
  • v1.2.1 (final, live) – Clearer finder arrows and a more prominent period result. Deployed to Google Cloud Run at https://spherexplorer-sky.study.

Try it: click "WISE 0855", then "Find SPHEREx images", then load frames in the SPHEREx images tab. You will see the coldest known brown dwarf in our Sun's neighbourhood appear only in SPHEREx's longest wavelengths.
